##Part B: Conditional Statements

##Question 1
```{r}
temp <- 33
if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
```

##Question 2
```{r}
age <- 17
if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
```

##Question 3
```{r}
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
```

##Question 4
```{r}
x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
# [1] "A"
# Why: x > 5 is TRUE, so R runs that branch and skips the rest.
# x > 8 is also TRUE, but it is never checked because an
# earlier condition already matched.
```

##Question 5
'if' tests one single TRUE/FALSE condition and runs a block of code, which can contain any number of statements. It errors on a vector condition (R 4.2 and later) or uses only the first element (older R). 'ifelse()' tests every element of a vector and returns a vector of the same length, picking a value for each element.
I choose if ... else for control flow on a single value, such as checking whether a file exists or running different code blocks. I choose ifelse() to create or recode a column of data.

##Part C

##Question 6
```{r}
file <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(file)) {
  grades <- read.csv(file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("File imported.")
} else {
  stop("File not found: ", file, ". Check getwd() or set the working directory.")
}
```

```{r}
nrow(grades); ncol(grades)
```

Rows and columns: 15 rows and 7 columns.
Missing values: one NA, in the Midterm column (the student with the missing midterm in the scenario). colSums above confirms it.
Section type: "character", because it holds the text A, B, or C.
Attendance range: range(grades$Attendance) gives the lowest and highest values.

```{r}
stopifnot(nrow(grades) == 15,
          ncol(grades) == 7,
          sum(is.na(grades)) == 1)
```

#f.1
```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final
```

#f.2
```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                 ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
```

#f.3
```{r}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair",
                         "Needs Improvement")))))
```

#f.4
```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
```

#f.5
```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) &
                        grades$FinalGrade >= 90 &
                        grades$Attendance >= 90,
                        "Yes", "No")
```

#f.6
```{r}
result_loop <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(grades))) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    result_loop[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    result_loop[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    result_loop[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

identical(result_loop, grades$Result)   
```

#f.7
```{r, error = TRUE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75)
  print("Passed")
```
grades$FinalGrade >= 75 produces a vector of 15 TRUE/FALSE/NA values, but if needs exactly one. In R 4.2 and later this is an error ("the condition has length > 1"). In older versions it is a warning that only the first element is used, so the other 14 students are silently ignored. If the value tested were the NA, you would also get "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". The loop avoids all of this by testing one element at a time and checking is.na() first.


##Part D: Exporting Results to .csv

##Question 7
```{r}
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No at-risk students. File not written.")
}
```

```{r}
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes",
                 c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No honors candidates. File not written.")
}
```

```{r}

all.equal(grades, check)                   # TRUE if identical
```


##Question 9
```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial",
                             "None")))

scholars <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]

if (nrow(scholars) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholars, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No scholarship candidates. File not written.")
}

table(grades$Scholarship)
```

##Question 10
```{r}
# 1. is.na() is checked first because comparing NA to a number gives NA,
#    not TRUE or FALSE. That would break if() with an error and make
#    ifelse() return NA instead of a proper label.

# 2. With "Failed" before "Incomplete", the NA grade would fail the
#    comparison (NA < 75 gives NA), so the student would end up with NA
#    instead of "Incomplete" (and in a plain if, R would stop with an error).

# 3. ifelse() is better for creating or recoding a whole column, since it
#    works on every element at once. if ... else is better for a single
#    TRUE/FALSE decision, such as "does the file exist?", or when each
#    branch runs several statements.

# 4. Reading the file back confirms it was written correctly (right rows,
#    columns, and values), so you catch problems before sending it to the registrar.
```
